ru: Я хочу́ поблагодари́ть вас за по́мощь.
en_alt: I want to thank you for the help.
note: The Russian has no possessive on «по́мощь», so the article variant is equally valid.
Perfective future is right; the partner's 'after the concert … in person' keeps the drill cue distinct.
The perfective 'thanked' is the correct half of this identical collision; the imperfective partner «Она́ благодари́ла учи́теля» is the side that should read 'was thanking'.

ru: Ты бы побыва́ла в Япо́нии с удово́льствием.
en_alt: You would visit Japan with pleasure.
note: Literal rendering of «с удово́льствием» added alongside 'gladly'.

en_alt: They have been to many countries.
note: «побыва́ть» in the past is idiomatically 'have been to'.

en_alt: I will visit Moscow in summer.
note: Article-free variant of the time phrase.

en_alt: He was lucky to find work.
note: «рабо́ту» is glossed 'work'; both renderings are accurate.

ru: Е́сли бы повезло́, мы бы вы́играли.
en_alt: If we had been lucky, we would have won.
note: бы+past licenses the past counterfactual too, and вы́играли is perfective.

en_alt: You will be lucky at the exam.
note: Preposition variant for «на экза́мене».

ru: Е́сли бы уви́дел сам, я пове́рил бы.
en: If I had seen it myself, I would have believed it.
note: Perfective пове́рить with бы is a completed past counterfactual; the imperfective partner «ты бы ему́ ве́рил» already holds the present 'would believe'.
Perfective future is correct here; the partner sentence about rumours carries its own lexical cue.

en: She came to believe in success.
note: Perfective пове́рить is inchoative; 'came to believe' reads as the single completed change of state and separates it from the imperfective partner's stative 'believed in success'.

ru: Е́сли бы услы́шал шум, я поверну́лся бы.
en_alt: If I heard a noise, I would turn around.
I would have turned around if I had heard a noise.
note: Word-order and past-counterfactual variants; бы+past licenses both readings.

en_alt: Will you turn towards the window?
note: «к окну́» is equally 'towards the window'.

en_alt: I will turn towards the window.
note: «к окну́» is equally 'towards the window'.

en: Soon she will turn towards us.
note: 'turn around towards us' is redundant; «повернётся к нам» is simply 'will turn towards us'.

en_alt: She will turn towards the sound.
note: «на звук» reads equally as 'towards the sound'.

en_alt: I would hang the picture a little higher.
note: по- on the comparative «повы́ше» means 'a little higher'.

ru: Я повторю́ э́то пра́вило ещё раз.
Е́сли ну́жно, я повтори́л бы вопро́с.
note: Frame-only collision, but the if-clause and object differ entirely from the imperfective partner's habitual 'forget and repeat mistakes'.
The imperative reads unmistakably against the partner's declarative present, so the shared 'repeat' frame is harmless.

en_alt: I will revise all the words tomorrow.
note: «повтори́ть слова́» is idiomatically 'revise' in a study context.

ru: Она́ повторя́ла оди́н и тот же сове́т.
Пе́ред экза́меном мы бу́дем повторя́ть грамма́тику.
note: 'revising' is the right sense of «повторя́ть грамма́тику», and the compound future is correctly rendered as a durative.
Frame-only collision against a perfective imperative; the cue is clear.

en_alt: Do you repeat the words?
note: The imperfective present covers both the habitual and the progressive reading.

ru: Без пра́ктики я бы забыва́л и повторя́л оши́бки.
note: Imperfective habitual 'would forget and repeat' is correct; the perfective partner is the single event.

ru: Я погляжу́ на но́вый дом за́втра.
Она́ погляде́ла на меня́ с улы́бкой.
Поглядя́т они́ на не́бо и улыбну́тся.
Ты бы погляде́ла на звёзды сего́дня.
en: You would take a look at the stars today.
note: Perfective погляде́ть is a single glance — 'take a look' — which also clears the shared 'would look' frame with the imperfective partner.

ru: Пока́ ты ведёшь маши́ну, я бу́ду погля́дывать на ка́рту.
en_alt: While you are driving, I will keep glancing at the map.
note: 'keep an eye on' is a good idiomatic rendering; the literal reading is added as an alternative.

ru: Он погля́дывал на дверь с трево́гой.
Ма́ма погля́дывает на дете́й во дворе́.
Я погля́дываю на часы́ ка́ждую мину́ту.
Я погля́дывала бы на часы́ от ску́ки.
Я поговорю́ с учи́телем по́сле уро́ка.
en_alt: I will talk with the teacher after the lesson.
note: Plain 'talk' is the natural alternative to 'have a talk'.

en_alt: I will talk to the director tomorrow.
note: Plain 'talk' is the natural alternative to 'have a talk'.

en_alt: Will you talk with me?
note: Plain 'talk' is the natural alternative to 'have a talk'.

en_alt: Let's talk about this tomorrow.
note: Plain 'talk' is the natural alternative to 'have a talk'.

ru: Я поговори́ла бы с ним споко́йно.
Во вре́мя пра́здника официа́нты бу́дут подава́ть обе́д на у́лице.
en: During the celebration, the waiters will be serving lunch outside.
note: The imperfective compound future бу́дут подава́ть is 'will be serving'; the flattened 'will serve' collided with the perfective «Они́ подаду́т у́жин в во́семь».

en_alt: The waiter is serving the soup.
note: The imperfective present covers both readings.

en_alt: We are submitting the documents tomorrow.
note: Scheduled-future reading of the imperfective present.

ru: Ты бы подава́ла чай в краси́вых ча́шках.
note: Imperfective бы+past is habitual here, so 'would serve' is right.

ru: Я подарю́ тебе́ кни́гу на день рожде́ния.
en_alt: I will give you a book for your birthday.
note: 'as a present' is implied by подари́ть; the shorter form is equally valid.

en_alt: Soon we will give him a bicycle as a present.
We will give him a bicycle soon.
note: 'as a present soon' is clumsy; fronting 'soon' reads better.

ru: Что мы пода́рим ма́ме на пра́здник?
en_alt: What will we give Mum as a present for the holiday?
note: 'shall'/'will' variant.
Model perfective past counterfactual — 'would have submitted'.

ru: За́втра она́ пода́ст докуме́нты в суд.
en_alt: Tomorrow she will submit the documents to the court.
note: Article variant.

en_alt: I will pass you the salt.
note: Uncontracted form, for the word-bank drill.
Perfective 'will serve dinner at eight' is correct; the imperfective partner is the side retranslated to 'will be serving'.

ru: Я поддержу́ тебя́ в тру́дный час.
en_alt: I will support you in a difficult hour.
I will support you in a hard time.
note: «тру́дный час» reads more naturally as 'a difficult hour' or 'a hard time'.
Frame-only collision; 'tomorrow … our proposal' keeps this distinct from the imperfective partner.
Frame-only collision with «всегда́ бу́ду подде́рживать»: 'will always be supporting' is not idiomatic English, and subject and object differ, so both sides stand.

ru: Ты бы поддержа́л э́ту иде́ю на собра́нии.
en_alt: You would have supported this idea at the meeting.
note: бы+past also licenses the past counterfactual.
Frame-only collision; the question form and 'my idea' distinguish it.

en_alt: They maintained contact for years.
note: 'kept in touch' is right; the literal reading is added as an alternative.

ru: Без тебя́ я бы не подде́рживала поря́док.
en_alt: Without you I would not keep the house in order.
Without you I would not maintain order.
note: 'keep order' on its own reads as keeping discipline; the alternatives track «подде́рживать поря́док».

en_alt: I keep order in the house.
note: 'keep' and 'maintain' are both accurate for подде́рживаю here.
'I will always be supporting you' is not idiomatic English, so the compound future stays as 'will always support'; all four perfective partners carry their own lexical cues.
Imperfective habitual 'would lift' is correct; the perfective partner «я по́днял бы коро́бку» is the side retranslated to 'would have lifted'.

en_alt: The crane is lifting a heavy load.
note: The imperfective present covers both readings.

en_alt: They were lifting the boxes up to the floor.
note: 'up to the floor' stops 'floor' being read as the ground.
Model imperfective compound future — 'will be lifting'.

ru: Мы поднима́емся на го́ру ка́ждое ле́то.
en_alt: We climb the mountain every summer.
note: Equally natural rendering of поднима́емся на го́ру.

ru: После́дние сто ме́тров мы бу́дем поднима́ться пешко́м.
en_alt: We will go up the last hundred metres on foot.
note: Matches the headword gloss 'to go up'.

ru: Я поднима́лась бы по ле́стнице пешко́м.
note: Imperfective habitual is correct; the perfective partner «я подня́лся бы вы́ше» is the side retranslated to a past counterfactual.

ru: Е́сли бы смог, я по́днял бы коро́бку.
en: I would have lifted the box if I could have.
note: Perfective по́днял бы is a completed past counterfactual; that leaves the imperfective partner «Я поднима́ла бы ме́ньше тя́жестей» as the only habitual 'would lift'.

en_alt: He picked up a stone from the ground.
note: «подня́ть с земли́» is idiomatically 'picked up'.

ru: За́втра мы подни́мем вопро́с о зарпла́те.
en_alt: Tomorrow we will raise the question of salary.
note: «зарпла́та» is glossed 'salary'.

ru: Ты бы по́днял э́ту те́му на собра́нии.
en_alt: You would have raised this topic at the meeting.
note: бы+past also licenses the past counterfactual.

en: I will lift this box myself.
note: 'raise a box' is not idiomatic English; подня́ть a box is 'lift'.

ru: Е́сли б не уста́л, я подня́лся бы вы́ше.
en: If I had not got tired, I would have gone higher.
note: Perfective подня́лся бы is a completed past counterfactual; that clears the shared 'would go' frame with the imperfective partner's habitual 'would go up the stairs'.

en_alt: Prices rose sharply over the year.
note: Equally natural rendering.

en_alt: Will you go up the mountain?
note: Matches the headword gloss 'to go up'.

ru: Мы подни́мемся на верши́ну к утру́.

en_alt: They will pick out a good suit for you.
note: 'pick out' tracks the headword gloss as well as 'select'.

en_alt: She picked up a kitten in the street.
note: British English prefers 'in the street'.
Frame-only collision; subject and object differ entirely from the imperfective partner.
Frame-only collision; the imperfective partner «Она́ ждала́ меня́ у вхо́да» is the side that should read 'was waiting'.

Identical to the imperfective «Жди меня́ у вхо́да»; English has no aspect contrast in the imperative, and подожди́ is the neutral form, so the fix belongs on the imperfective side (e.g. 'Keep waiting for me at the entrance') rather than here.

ru: Ско́ро я подожду́ тебя́ у вхо́да.
note: «Ско́ро я подожду́ тебя́ у вхо́да» is stilted — announcing a short future wait with «ско́ро» is not idiomatic; a native would say «Я подожду́ тебя́ у вхо́да».

en_alt: The girl went up to the teacher.
note: «подойти́ к» is idiomatically 'go up to'.

en_alt: He went up to the window.
note: «подойти́ к» is idiomatically 'go up to'.

en_alt: Will you come over to the window?
note: «подойти́ к» is idiomatically 'come over to'.

ru: Ско́ро официа́нт подойдёт к на́шему сто́лику.
en_alt: Soon the waiter will come over to our table.
note: 'come over to' is what a waiter does; added alongside the literal 'approach'.

ru: Ты бы подошёл к нему́ пе́рвым.
note: Frame-only collision; subject and adverb differ from the imperfective partner's 'more carefully'.

ru: Я подойду́ к тебе́ по́сле уро́ка.
en_alt: I will come up to you after the lesson.
note: 'approach you' is stiff here; the idiomatic reading is added as an alternative.

ru: Я подписа́л письмо́ и отпра́вил его́.

en_alt: Sign here, please.
note: Matches the Russian word order.

ru: Я подписа́ла бы догово́р без коле́баний.
en_alt: I would have signed the contract without hesitation.
note: бы+past also licenses the past counterfactual.
